title.narrative: PPP for Sustainable Water supply: Ridge to Coast, Rain to Tap

description.narrative: The ‘Ridge to Coast, Rain to Tap’ (R2CR2T) project aims to address several identified factors in order to reduce flood vulnerability and improve the resilience of the water supply in Cagayan de Oro, the Philippines.The project, which started on 1st January 2018, has adopted an integrated approach, working both directly on the water supply infrastructure and at a systemic level in the river basin. Through capacity development, investments and technical assistance, the project will provide a strong boost to improve the operations of the Cagayan de Oro Water District (COWD). This includes integration of several IT tools, among which GIS and hydraulic modelling, in COWD’s operations. Water supply coverage, sanitation services and disaster risk reduction are being expanded to up to 7,000 previously unserved households in relocation areas and four nearby schools, mostly consisting of residents who lost their homes in the 2011 Sendong flood. In the upstream Cagayan de Oro River Basin (CDORB), several pilot reforestation interventions are being implemented in partnership with local Indigenous Peoples (IP) communities to demonstrate effective and sustainable ways for addressing the causes of flooding. The project aims to contribute to an enabling environment in which public and private stakeholders in CDO and Bukidnon Province cooperate towards flood risk reduction.The R2CR2T project is a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) including partners Cagayan de Oro Water District, VEI, FITC, Unifrutti Tropical Philippines Inc, Cagayan de Oro River Basin Management Council, Hineleban Foundation, Bukidnon Indigenous Peoples Advisory Council, Wetlands International, the Philippines Red Cross and the Netherlands Red Cross.The R2CR2T project is 49% co-funded by the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and administered by the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) through the Sustainable Water Fund.

The income generated from SDIC adlai sales by indigenous farmers in Lirongan and labor payments for tree planting in Lirongan are counted as direct jobs created. These were both lower in 2021 and 2022 compared to 2020, since the highest volume of tree planting and adlai sales were recorded in 2020. The targets set for total FTE created at the start of the project (i.e. 100 FTE for reforestation activities and SDIC income annually) seem to have been an over-estimation: these will not be achieved.
This is the total target for the project

comment.narrative: 2023: PW's 1, 4, 7, 9, 19, 24, 30 now all considered flood resilient. The same notes apply as in 2022: for PWs 4, 7, 19, 30 resilience depends on COWD's timely evacuation of the gensets, while for PW's 19 and 24 it depends on the installation of gate valves on the sluice gates
2024: Sluice gates have been equipped with gate valves

PW's 1, 19 & 24 considered flood resilient. Note: this resilience is based on the assumption that flood wall Balulang is water-proof and that sluice valves for local drains there can be closed in case of flooding (which was not the case in Aug 2022) Mobile carts PW9 & 30 rehabilitated, so also considered flood resilient. PWs 4 & 7: no measures implemented: these remain vulnerable to flooding.
This is the total target for the project
